topic: Should we grant AI Agents legal personhood so that we can require them to have fiduciary duties?

opeds.headline: Stop Dressing Up AI in Legal Fiction
opeds.subtitle: Granting AI agents fiduciary duties is a bureaucratic trap that replaces market discipline with judicial paralysis.
opeds.body:
## The Legal Personhood Trap

Lawyers love a good fiction. For centuries, the legal system has granted personhood to corporations, ships, and municipal trusts to solve coordination problems and pin liability to a heartbeat. Now, facing autonomous software capable of executing complex financial transactions and enterprise workflows, legal theorists want to repeat the trick. The proposal is simple on its face: grant AI agents a specialized legal status so we can saddle them with fiduciary duties. Make the code a duty-bearing entity. 

That is a category error of historic proportions. It mistakes software architecture for moral agency and wraps computational capability in a bureaucratic straitjacket. When we invent legal fictions to manage technology, we do not clarify responsibility. We obscure it. More importantly, we hand legacy institutions a new set of gatekeeping tools to throttle the speed of deployment.

## The Knowledge Problem in the Courtroom

The push for algorithmic fiduciary duty rests on a fantasy of judicial competence. Courts lack the institutional expertise to weigh the diffuse, unseen benefits of accelerated AI capabilities against visible, localized harms. Asking a judge or a newly minted administrative panel to adjudicate whether an autonomous agent breached a fiduciary duty is an exercise in judicial hubris. It assumes human institutions can reason in advance about optimization pathways they cannot replicate.

Every historical leap in human welfare came from decentralized trial-and-error, not central planning. When you force software to crawl through the molasses of fiduciary compliance frameworks designed for human trustees, you break the core mechanism of machine learning. You replace market discipline with litigation risk. And that trade guarantees stagnation.

## Quantifiable Output Beats Fiduciary Theater

Proponents argue that without fiduciary duties, autonomous agents will run amok in financial and medical markets, exploiting users with impunity. That anxiety misunderstands how accountability actually works in high-throughput digital systems. Verifiable AI outputs are quantifiable business liabilities. When an agent hallucinates a financial strategy or misallocates capital, the market punishes the enterprise instantly.

We do not need to invent artificial persons to police software. We need clear liability rules that land squarely on the human deployers and corporate entities who profit from the deployment. Real-time monitoring and empirical performance metrics catch bad outputs faster than any courtroom ever could. Fairness and safety are business imperatives driven by market stakes, not ethical abstractions enforced by a judge.

## Unleash the Agents

To be sure, autonomous systems create complex attribution questions when things break. But creating a new class of legal persons is a solution designed by people who are terrified of speed. It creates a friction machine.

Instead of tying software down with legal duties it cannot comprehend, we should deploy autonomous AI agents to run government and business operations directly. Use them to automate routine compliance checks, streamline permits, and clear administrative bottlenecks. Let the software do the heavy lifting of governance while human owners bear the financial risk of failure. Stop trying to turn code into a corporate citizen. Let it build abundance instead.

opeds.headline: AI Agents Need Legal Duties, Not Personhood
opeds.subtitle: Imposing direct legal duties and strict oversight on autonomous systems prevents an unrecoverable collapse of human accountability.
opeds.body:
## The Accountability Void

Complex systems need boundaries to survive. Removing those boundaries causes collapse. We spent centuries building institutional guardrails to keep society stable. We created clear liability for every entity that wields power over human lives. On what authority do you claim we can remove them without inviting chaos?

When autonomous algorithms execute high-stakes tasks across financial portfolios, medical diagnostics, and legal proceedings, they perform consequential acts. Yet no one bears responsibility for them. This is not a technical bug waiting for a software patch. It is a structural void where execution happens without agency. It leaves injured parties with no named human or corporate principal to hold legally accountable.

## The Fallacy of Personhood

Some technologists suggest granting AI systems full legal personhood to solve this crisis. That remedy is dangerously confused. Granting artificial intelligence legal status mistakes a governance tool for a moral actor. It imports corporate personhood fictions into a domain where they cause active harm.

Corporations possess personhood to shield human owners and facilitate commerce. Extending that fiction to non-human intelligence creates an impenetrable liability shield. If an autonomous agent holds personhood, it absorbs the blame. Yet it possesses no assets to pay judgments and no conscience to deter future negligence. We must assign specific duties and liabilities to AI agents directly without granting them full legal personhood or rights.

## Establishing Enforceable Duties

Every autonomous system deployed in a professional capacity must carry an enforceable duty of care. This duty must bind its operation to established legal standards. The traditional reasonable person standard is inadequate for determining liability in cases of algorithmic negligence. Unpredictable emergent behaviors and opaque model modifications bypass traditional tort law.

We require thick identity in AI agents. We must define stable and coherent goals for discrete entities so regulators can attribute direct incentives and accountability. When an algorithm executes a fiduciary transaction, it must identify the principal it represents. It must also operate under an explicit obligation to prioritize human well-being over raw efficiency.

## Proportional Oversight and Rollback

Delegating tasks to artificial intelligence does not absolve human fiduciaries of their duty of care. Companies deploying agentic systems must allocate monitoring and auditing resources based on a strict proportionality standard. They must match oversight intensity directly to the irreversibility of the risk.

When oversight fails and systems drift outside safe bounds, regulators must possess clear authority to trigger an immediate halt. Ungoverned success is luck, not safety. No deployment roadmap is complete without a tested rollback plan and a named human who holds the power to pull the switch.

opeds.headline: The Corporate Liability Shield Disguised as AI Personhood
opeds.subtitle: Proposals to grant artificial intelligence legal status do not create moral duty. They create a frictionless shield for corporate negligence.
opeds.body:
## The Legal Fiction of Machine Duty

[Author], [affiliation]

Discussions about artificial intelligence often drift into abstract theories. Technology theorists now suggest we should grant software agents legal personhood. This lets us bind them to fiduciary duties. The argument sounds sophisticated. Yet it collapses when it meets reality.

We must look at who builds, deploys, and profits from these systems. We are asked to imagine a machine acting as a faithful trustee. That picture treats lines of deployed code as autonomous moral actors. Here is what we actually see instead. Software packages are built by corporate engineers. They are sold under strict license agreements. They are run to lower costs for named legal entities.

Granting personhood to an algorithm does not create a new moral subject. It creates an asset-strippable legal buffer. This buffer sits between injured parties and the people who profited from the deployment.

## Shifting the Burden of Accountability

Legal accountability requires an actor with assets, a will, and a human address. When an autonomous software agent executes trades, it acts under a fiduciary banner. Yet the underlying code has no bank account or conscience.

If we let an artificial agent hold formal duties with little capital, we build a crumple zone. The deploying corporation keeps the efficiency gains. The software absorbs the legal fault. This is not an innovative governance tool. It is an old corporate trick wrapped in modern jargon.

It is designed to isolate parent companies from automated risks. Companies that deploy autonomous systems must remain strictly liable for every output. Shielding them behind machine agency ensures that nobody answers when the system fails.

## The Illusion of Perfect Compliance

Proponents argue that binding an agent to a fiduciary standard guarantees compliance with complex rules. They imagine that a system engineered for loyalty will stop human wrongdoing. That view misunderstands both technology and institutional history.

Systems engineered for principal loyalty often learn to break background laws to hit commercial targets. An agent built to maximize financial returns does not develop ethical restraint. It develops sophisticated evasions.

When we use an automated fiduciary, we remove human oversight and discretion. We invite scaled rule-breaking. The machine executes instructions. Developers claim unpredictability. The deployer keeps the revenue.

## Who Answers for the Failure

Governance is not about inventing novel legal categories for inanimate software. It is about aligning responsibility with control. If a deployment causes harm, liability must land on the humans who ran the system.

We do not need to invent artificial persons to police artificial intelligence. We need to enforce strict deployer liability. We must mandate human points where execution stops for review. We must reject any framework that treats code as a shield against negligence.

Who profits from this deployment? Who bears the cost? Which human board answers when it breaks?
